cells.tense: You are here, standing in what a group hands down together.
cells.ask: Name the one thing you keep alive on purpose, and say who you keep it for.
cells.core:
You have a hand on what gets handed down, and the hand is steady. Not because you hold tight, but because you can tell when a thing has been carried long enough to set down. Your part in it is clear, and so is the point where your part stops.

What you hold together holds because you are not forcing it. You give what you have to the room and let the room answer. That is the whole of it, and it is rare. Spend some of what you keep on whoever comes next. The hand stays steady when it steadies someone else.
cells.sheetLine: You carry what is worth carrying, and you know when to hand it off.
cells.verb: handing over what is worth keeping
cells.place: the room where a tradition is carried and passed on

cells.tense: You are bracing for a future that has not arrived and cannot be written in advance.
cells.ask: Say a thing once to the group, then spend one afternoon leaving it alone to see if it stands.
cells.core:
You are ahead of the room, guarding something no one has threatened. You can picture the version where it goes wrong, and you are already living there, tightening what has not loosened. Every shared thing turns into a load you keep intact by yourself.

That kind of guarding is not the same as care, and people feel the difference. They stop adding to what you keep, because you have shown them their hands are not needed. The thing you are trying to keep alive keeps getting smaller, and it is your grip doing the shrinking. A lighter hand lets it breathe.
cells.sheetLine: You are holding it so hard it has stopped being shared.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that closed behind you some time back.
cells.ask: Pick one small thing your group already does and join it fully this week, no explaining why.
cells.core:
You can see what gets passed around the room and you have not reached out for it. The distance looks like respect from the outside. From in here it looks like standing at the edge, waiting for a reason to step in that does not come.

What you have is enough to give, and no one is asking you to be more than one set of hands. Pick a practice someone started before you and take it up. Belonging is built in the doing, not in getting your standing settled first.
cells.sheetLine: You have a place in what is shared, and you have not taken it up.

cells.tense: You are shaping what gets passed on right now, with the pen already down.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you already do that keeps a tradition going, and call it yours in front of one person.
cells.core:
You are keeping something going that you did not start, and you have not said so. You carry the language, the timing, the small habits that hold a group together. When people ask how it works, you point at the thing itself, as if it were running on its own.

Someone taught you that keeping quiet about your part is the same as humility. It is not. The people around you cannot see what you are holding, so they cannot join you in it, and the thing you tend stays smaller than it could be. What you have kept is worth saying out loud.
cells.sheetLine: You are keeping something alive and calling it nobody's doing.

attempts.check: The draft wants to say the person is exhausted by guardianship, but nothing in the record shows fatigue, only the mechanism of over-direction. The reader could reasonably object that they are not holding anything, or have never been trusted with what is shared. The ask survives being wrong: saying a piece once and letting it stand is useful for anyone, whether they are over-governing or simply have not spoken yet. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line that flatters the reader as the one person who ever kept the whole thing alive.
